 Addressing supporters after midnight, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, who leads a bloc of opposition parties, both expressed confidence that they will lead Israel’s next government. Vote counting could take days.
 Published Oct. 27, 2026 Updated Oct. 28, 2026, 1:39 a.m. ET Share full article 
 Video Israeli exit polls showed early Wednesday that the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, was roughly even with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc, with neither winning a parliamentary majority. Credit Credit... By Alisa Shodiyev Kaff 
 Key Players › Benjamin Netanyahu
 Prime minister and leader of far-right coalition
 Gadi Eisenkot
 Center-right former military chief
 Itamar Ben-Gvir
 Far-right national security minister
 Naftali Bennett

 Follow live updates on the Israeli election here . 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda. Add The New York Times on Google Agrega The New York Times en Google 
 Latest
 Pinned David M. Halbfinger Max Bearak Isabel Kershner Aaron Boxerman and Johnatan Reiss 
 Here’s the latest. 
 Israelis voted in the largest numbers in a generation on Tuesday, and exit polls suggested that a bloc of opposition parties was roughly even with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance in what many described as a make-or-break moment for the nation.
 The election did not appear to immediately determine who would lead the country next, even as the leading candidates — Mr. Netanyahu and the leader of a coalition of opposition parties, Gadi Eisenkot — struck tones of victory in late-night addresses to supporters. Vote counting was expected to last days, followed by a potentially lengthy effort by the blocs to assemble a parliamentary majority.
 The exit polls, if accurate, suggest that neither Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc nor the one led by Mr. Eisenkot , a former military chief whose son was killed in the Gaza war, will be able to form a government without relying on two Arab parties that were projected to win as many as 17 or 18 seats in Parliament. Mr. Netanyahu effectively ruled out including them in a governing coalition, and Mr. Eisenkot and his partners have balked at the idea, too.
 One option analysts are already weighing is whether Mr. Netanyahu, who has led the most far-right government in Israeli history, could join with Mr. Eisenkot or others in the opposition to form a unity government. But a unity government would face major obstacles, given how deeply Mr. Eisenkot’s voters despise Mr. Netanyahu, and because the two would have to agree on which of them would serve as prime minister. Mr. Netanyahu is unlikely to give up control, while Mr. Eisenkot has called the prime minister unfit to lead Israel.
 Much remained unclear early Wednesday morning in Israel. Making matters even murkier, Israel’s exit polls have a spotty history of accuracy, particularly in tight races.
 Mr. Eisenkot appeared onstage past midnight at his post-election party and attempted to strike a tone of triumph — as well as defiance toward Mr. Netanyahu.
 “Tonight we got the answer: The public wants change,” he said.
 Mr. Netanyahu addressed his supporters a few hours later, invoking his relationship with President Trump and repeating his pre-election talking points about removing the threat of Iran. He sounded triumphant, saying it was clear that Likud had emerged as the largest party in Israel and mocking months of pre-election polls that showed his party trailing behind that of Mr. Eisenkot.
 “We must form a strong right-wing government,” he declared.
 In the coming days, after official vote totals are released and parliamentary seats are allocated to parties, Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will invite the party leader he thinks has the best chance to assemble a governing coalition. Such a coalition would usually have to be made up of at least 61 lawmakers, though Mr. Eisenkot has floated the idea of forming a minority government.
 One factor not reflected in exit polls are the hundreds of thousands of votes cast by Israelis at special polling stations, including at military bases, hospitals, prisons and embassies. In the previous election, those votes tended to favor the coalition of Mr. Netanyahu and his allies.
 Here’s what else to know:
 Arab parties: The exit polls pointed to at least one surprise in projecting that two Arab parties would win as many as 17 or 18 seats in the 120-seat Parliament. That would be their strongest showing ever, and potentially give them an important role in forming the next government. Read more › 
 War fears: Amid reports that Mr. Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Mr. Eisenkot warned him in his speech to supporters not to abuse his power as caretaker prime minister to influence the process of forming a new government. “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” he said.
 Show more Oct. 27, 2026, 9:55 p.m. ET Johnatan Reiss 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv It’s nearly 4 a.m. in Israel, and there is no clear winner. News is expected to slow down in the coming hours, but pick up again in the morning, when party leaders are expected to begin discussing potential alliances. The official results are still a long way off: Election authorities have so far counted nearly a million votes, about a fifth of the total votes cast.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 9:40 p.m. ET Isabel Kershner 
 Reporting from Jerusalem In a nod to the fact he is now a caretaker prime minister pending the formation of a new government, Netanyahu said the exit polls were only a preview and he was waiting for official results. Yet he sounded triumphant, if not quite saying he had won the election. He said it was clear that his Likud party had emerged as the largest party in the Parliament, and he mocked months of pre-election polls that showed Likud trailing behind the party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot.
 Four Ways Israel’s Election Could End. Eventually.
 No party is expected to achieve a clear victory, which means the election will likely only be the first step in determining who will form the next government. Here’s how that might unfold.

 Hebron, West Bank Israeli settlers and border police officers lining up to vote. Leo Correa/Associated Press

 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 9:37 p.m. ET Isabel Kershner 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Listing Israel’s enemies who have now been killed, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei of Iran, Netanyahu declared, “Iran is weaker than ever, Israel is stronger than ever.”
 “But it’s still not over,” he said, adding that with his “friend” President Trump, it would be possible to remove the threat from Iran once and for all, repeating his pre-election talking points.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 9:35 p.m. ET Isabel Kershner 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Netanyahu showed no hint of extending a hand to the opposition as he addressed supporters early Wednesday. Arriving onstage at 3:15 a.m., looking reinvigorated and in an ebullient mood, he declared, “We must form a strong right-wing government.”
 Image Credit... Ronen Zvulun/Reuters Oct. 27, 2026, 8:52 p.m. ET Johnatan Reiss 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv One updated exit poll has given Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc a small edge over the opposition. The exit polls by Israel’s three largest television networks at first projected a small lead for Gadi Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu alliance, but now one has Netanyahu and his allies ahead, and the other two show the two blocs even. Exit polls have not always been reliable indicators of the result, and the official count is far from complete. But it appears that neither side has a clear path to forming a government without the help of the Arab parties, unless one or more parties defects from one of the main blocs. 
 Oct. 27, 2026, 7:53 p.m. ET Isabel Kershner 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, took the stage in the early hours of Wednesday morning like a winner, embracing members of his Yashar party who were waiting for him there and waving to an enthusiastic crowd of flag-waving supporters who hailed him as the next prime minister. 
 Although Eisenkot’s path to forming a government is far from clear, he gave what amounted to a victory speech for the opposition bloc, declaring, “We’ve made history.” Describing the election as a referendum on who should lead Israel in the coming years, he added: “Tonight we got the answer. The public wants change.”
 In an unusual and pointed message, Eisenkot told the country’s security chiefs and public servants that Netanyahu now heads a transitional government that has lost the confidence of the people. “Stand strong and firm against any attempt to challenge you,” Eisenkot said. “You have my clear backing.” Amid reports that Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Eisenkot said, “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs.”
 Video Credit Credit... Associated Press Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 7:53 p.m. ET Johnatan Reiss 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv Two Israeli news channels have recently updated their exit polls, which now show a tie between the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that of his main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot. Neither bloc, however, has enough seats to form a government without the support of Arab parties. Earlier versions of the same exit polls had shown small leads for the opposition alliance. The official vote count is still too preliminary to draw any conclusions, and counting will take days.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 7:50 p.m. ET Liam Stack 
 A strong showing by two Arab parties could give them a role in the formation of the next government. 
 Image Supporters of Israel’s Arab-led Joint List political alliance cheering as the first exit polls are announced on Tuesday. Credit... Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images One of the most striking results from the election in Israel on Tuesday was the unusually strong showing by two leading Arab parties, whose voters turned out in record numbers to express their opposition to the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
 The final results have not been announced, but a range of exit polls conducted by Israeli broadcasters suggest that two of the parties — the socially conservative United Arab List, or Raam, and the left-wing Joint List — may have won a historically large number of seats in parliament and an important role in the formation of the country’s next government.
 Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, told a television interviewer that the turnout showed that Arab voters, who make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population, had channeled their “frustration and despair” into “hope.”
 He said he wanted to replace Mr. Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way” and that his first priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” that achieved that goal.
 The Arab parties’ strong showing may make them kingmakers. But building a governing coalition with Arab participation remains a fraught exercise in Israel. Many Israeli Jews believe that a parliamentary majority should not rely on the support of Arab lawmakers.
 Image People waiting to cast ballots in Umm al-Fahm, one of the largest Arab towns in Israel, on Tuesday. Credit... Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Most Arab citizens are the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homes during the 1948 Arab-Israel war at the time of Israel’s independence.
 Today, they mostly live in separate towns from Jewish Israelis and face violence and discriminatory housing policies.
 Over the decades, disagreements, including over Israel’s nature as a Jewish state, have led many Arab voters to avoid the ballot box. 
 This week, many Arab voters said they were furious at Mr. Netanyahu for his treatment of the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and for policies that they feel treat Palestinians in Israel as second-class citizens. Indeed, throughout the campaign, Mr. Netanyahu made overt appeals to anti-Arab prejudice.
 Of the two Arab parties that did well on Tuesday, only Raam has joined a coalition government in the past. That happened in 2021, when it joined the short-lived anti-Netanyahu coalition of Prime Minister Naftali Bennett.
 Raam’s participation in that government outraged many right-wing Jewish voters, and when it collapsed after roughly one year, they backed Mr. Netanyahu, who went on to form the most hard-line government in Israel’s history.
 That government now faces the possibility that it may be brought down by an election result that has been deeply shaped by robust Arab turnout.
 Show more Oct. 27, 2026, 7:38 p.m. ET Natan Odenheimer 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Scores of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s supporters and lawmakers from his Likud party are gathered at the party’s election-night headquarters, in a conference hall in Jerusalem. It’s past 1:30 a.m., and some of the crowd here is ecstatic, waiting for the prime minister to come and speak onstage. Activists are wearing “Make Israel Great Again” baseball hats and throwing the party’s voting slips like confetti. But others, including party officials, acknowledged to me their path to forming a coalition is narrow, and feelings here are mixed.
 Video Credit Credit... Natan Odenheimer/The New York Times Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 7:10 p.m. ET Isabel Kershner 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Bezalel Smotrich, the current finance minister and leader of the far-right Religious Zionism party, focused his post-election speech on delegitimizing the predominantly Arab parties whose support could help the anti-Netanyahu bloc form a government. “Parties that are unable to condemn the massacre of Oct. 7 and are not willing to declare Hamas as a terrorist organization are not legitimate actors in Israeli politics,” Smotrich told his supporters.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 7:04 p.m. ET Johnatan Reiss 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv Naftali Bennett, who leads a party in the alliance opposing Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc, said the sitting prime minister had lost the election. In a fiery televised address to a gathering of supporters, he tied Netanyahu to the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, Israel’s worst security failure in decades. “The government of Oct. 7 will go home,” he said.
 He said the anti-Netanyahu parties “will do everything, setting ego aside” to form a government that will insist on conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews into the military. He did not address whether that might include Netanyahu’s Likud party, or one or more Arab parties.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 6:30 p.m. ET Johnatan Reiss 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv Not reflected in exit polls are hundreds of thousands of ballots cast at special polling stations, including on military bases, in hospitals, prisons, and embassies. In the previous election, those votes leaned toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition. This year, the election authorities estimated that roughly 600,000 such votes would be cast, accounting for about 10 percent of eligible voters. Results from those ballots are not expected to be announced before Thursday.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 6:01 p.m. ET Johnatan Reiss 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, was the first leader of a party in Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition to speak following tonight’s exit polls. He neither declared victory for his bloc nor conceded defeat. “The night is still young,” he told supporters at a televised gathering. He said he hoped that the bloc led by Netanyahu “was close to forming a right-wing government.”
 Image Credit... Ilia Yefimovich/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 5:47 p.m. ET Heedo Abu Laban 
 Reporting from Lod, Israel The leader of the Democrats party, Yair Golan, declared victory on Tuesday night for the opposition bloc, which includes his party, and asserted that the exit polls showed that the Israeli public had “fired Netanyahu and Likud.” Addressing supporters, Golan urged opposition leaders to swiftly form a “change government” without letting ego or political calculations delay the process. “From tonight, Israel can breathe,” he said. “Tomorrow, we begin rebuilding.” He expressed a willingness to rely on support from outside the opposition alliance to secure a parliamentary majority, an apparent reference to the Arab parties.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 5:44 p.m. ET David Halbfinger 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Another surprise in the exit polls was Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s apparent surge on Election Day. While the most recent pre-election surveys showed his Likud party with about 20 seats in Parliament, the exit polls show Likud winning 24, more than any other party. That is an important symbolic victory for Netanyahu, and one that few could have foreseen for the prime minister who was in charge on Oct. 7, 2023.
 It suggests that Netanyahu’s hair-on-fire appeal to voters on Election Day worked — but only so much. The extra four seats he picked up, according to the exit polls, came at the expense of his allies, not the opposition bloc.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 5:42 p.m. ET David Halbfinger 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Judging by exit polls, one major suprise in this election is the high turnout among Israel’s Arab citizens, who were furious at the current government over its housing policies and its failure to curb violent crime in Arab communities. 
 Pre-election surveys suggested that the two main Arab parties would win about 13 seats, but the exit polls suggest they will end up with closer to 17 or 18 seats. In the past, Arab parties have never won more than 15.
 Mansour Abbas, the leader of the Raam party, told a television interviewer on Tuesday night that the turnout showed that “frustration and despair” in Israel’s Arab society had “turned to hope.”
 Oct. 27, 2026, 5:42 p.m. ET Johnatan Reiss 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv Mansour Abbas, the leader of an Arab party that could prove pivotal to the opposition’s efforts to form a majority coalition, said he wanted to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way.” In an interview with Israel’s Channel 12, he said his immediate priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” opposed to Netanyahu. “And then, we will discuss the details,” he said, “and address the challenges.”
 Image Credit... Mahmoud Illean/Associated Press Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 5:27 p.m. ET Adam Rasgon 
 Reporting from Haifa, Israel Initial exit polls suggest that Arab parties are likely to win a historic number of seats in Israel’s Parliament.
 The polls released by Israeli TV channels gave Raam and the Joint List, the two major Arab parties, either 17 or 18 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
 “The Arabs feel this government did everything to marginalize them and even incite against them,” said Thabet Abu Ras, an expert in Arab-Jewish relations and an Arab citizen of Israel. “They understood they needed to fight for their citizenship and play the political game fully.”
 Oct. 27, 2026, 5:22 p.m. ET Aaron Boxerman 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Israel’s Central Election Committee just updated the country’s turnout rate to 77.7 percent, the highest since 1999. Israelis headed in large numbers to the polls on Tuesday, particularly among the country’s Arab minority, who were spurred by a desire to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu’s hardline coalition.
 Image Credit... David Goldman/Associated Press Oct. 27, 2026, 5:19 p.m. ET Yair Rosenberg 
 In 2021, Israel’s short-lived anti-Netanyahu government included for the first time an independent Arab party, Raam. The backlash to that catapulted anti-Arab politicians like Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich into the next government. According to exit polls, the backlash to that government appears to have resulted today in a record showing for Israel’s Arab parties.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 5:05 p.m. ET Aaron Boxerman 
 Reporting from Jerusalem The exit polls suggest Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition may well be deadlocked with his Jewish opponents, and neither would be able to form a government on their own without relying on Arab parties. One option already being weighed by analysts is whether Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, could form a unity government of Israel’s right-wing and centrist parties. Such an alliance might be hard for Eisenkot to accept given how deeply his own voters despise Netanyahu. And then there’s also the question of who would run the government. Netanyahu is unlikely to give up control, and Eisenkot has vowed not to join a government run by someone he has called unfit to lead Israel.
 Image Credit... Shir Torem/Reuters Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 4:53 p.m. ET Isabel Kershner 
 Reporting from Jerusalem There have been precedents in the past where the party with the most seats in Parliament does not end up forming a government. In Israel’s 2009 election, Tzipi Livni’s centrist Kadima party won 28 seats, narrowly beating Benjamin Netanyahu’s conservative Likud, which won 27. But Netanyahu had more support from allied parties and came back as prime minister after a decade spent out of politics or in the opposition.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 4:52 p.m. ET Natan Odenheimer 
 Reporting from Jerusalem A few activists were celebrating at the Likud Party’s election headquarters in Jerusalem even though most exit polls suggested that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance of parties had won fewer seats than the bloc of parties seeking his ouster. “Bibi is the king! The king is Bibi!” they shouted, using a nickname for the Israeli leader.
 Video Credit Credit... Natan Odenheimer/The New York Times Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 3:49 p.m. ET Liam Stack 
 What to expect now that the polls have closed in Israel. 
 Image A voter casting a ballot in Jerusalem. Credit... Ohad Zwigenberg/Associated Press Polls have closed in Israel, and initial exit polls by Israeli broadcasters are expected to be released shortly afterward. But it will be hours before the definitive results are known, and it could be weeks until a new government is formed. 
 Here’s what to know:
 Early indicator: Exit polls in Israel can be useful to get a sense of each party’s relative strength, but they are not considered a reliable gauge of precise results — particularly in a tight race like this one.
 Vote-counting: Votes are tallied in Israel by hand, with ballot slips tabulated at more than 12,000 polling places across the country. The counters are monitored by camera-toting election observers.
 First results: After the hand count is completed, paper tallies are taken to regional hubs where the results are recorded electronically. The whole process takes hours, and the authorities begin to release the results once they are completed. 
 Possible delay: Israel is a parliamentary democracy, and no party is expected to win anywhere near an outright majority of the votes. Once the results are in, the process of forming a government will begin. That could take weeks or even months.
 Next government: The party with the most votes and the most seats in the Parliament may not be the one to form a government. In 2021, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party won the most seats but was unable to assemble a majority coalition. Instead, after months of wrangling, an eclectic coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces cobbled together a single-seat majority in Parliament. 
 Oct. 27, 2026, 3:45 p.m. ET Leo Sands 
 Twice before, Netanyahu was ousted then returned to power. 
 Image Benjamin Netanyahu, shown in 2025, is already Israel’s longest-serving prime minister by far and is seeking a seventh term. Credit... Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing coalition has the distinction of surviving for a full four-year term in office, something no government in Israel has achieved for more than 30 years. Since first taking office in 1996, he has tallied 19 years in power and become Israel’s longest-serving prime minister by far.
 On Tuesday, he is seeking a seventh term, in Israel’s first parliamentary election since the deadly Hamas-led attack in 2023 that prompted its devastating war in Gaza.
 The longevity of his most recent governing coalition followed three years during which a cycle of collapsed coalitions and five snap elections had left the country without a functional government or national budget. 
 In 2021, Israelis ousted Mr. Netanyahu from power and then returned him to office 18 months later. He had staged a previous comeback, in 2009, becoming prime minister a decade after his party was voted out of power. 
 March 2021
 Ousted by a single-seat majority
 In 2021, Mr. Netanyahu’s government collapsed after failing to pass a budget, setting off legislative elections. At the time, he had been indicted on charges of fraud, bribery and breach of trust , and the coalition he was leading was shaky. According to analysts , heading into an election was a gambit by Mr. Netanyahu to strengthen his grip on power before his criminal trial.
 But the electorate that voted that March didn’t give him the seats he needed, ending a period of 12 straight years in office for him. It took months of wrangling for an eclectic coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces to cobble together a single-seat majority in the Parliament. Naftali Bennett, a right-wing former ally of Mr. Netanyahu’s, led the coalition as prime minister, hammering out a deal with Yair Lapid, a centrist and former broadcaster who was appointed foreign minister.
 The eight-party coalition proved too unwieldy to endure. After two right-wing lawmakers defected and several on the left rebelled in critical votes, that government collapsed in June 2022 .
 November 2022
 Returned to office by a hard-line coalition
 After the resulting elections, held in November 2022, Mr. Netanyahu returned to power as right-wing voters moved to more extreme parties, diminishing the center left.
 Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party allied with far-right and ultra-Orthodox lawmakers to secure a clear majority in the Parliament , forming the most hard-line and religious conservative government in Israel’s history.
 The coalition accounted for 48.4 percent of the vote but had a parliamentary majority because two anti-Netanyahu parties — one leftist, one Arab nationalist — fell just short of the share of votes needed to obtain seats.
 It was a reminder of how tiny swings among voters can have a big effect under Israel’s parliamentary system.
 Mr. Netanyahu has since overseen an acceleration of the country’s rightward shift, including an effort to overhaul the judiciary that prompted huge street protests. Questions about whether his government could have better pre-empted the Oct. 7 attack have also become hot-button issues .
 In April, Mr. Lapid and Mr. Bennett said they would reconstitute their centrist alliance of 2021 for the 2026 election. Mr. Netanyahu will also face Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who leads the largest opposition party .
 Show more Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 3:30 p.m. ET Isabel Kershner 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Israel’s economic future is on the ballot after Netanyahu offers a grim forecast. 
 Image Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has argued that Israel’s economy is healthy, but warned that its financial isolation could deepen. Credit... Ammar Awad/Reuters Days before Tuesday’s pivotal Israeli election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shocked his country by offering a bleak economic forecast that critics said could make Israel more like Iran, Russia and North Korea.
 Mr. Netanyahu told an Israeli financial journalist on Friday that he was preparing for international sanctions against Israeli banks by drawing up plans for a “bypass economy” based on cryptocurrency. He also told Israelis to prepare for the end of billions of dollars of annual American assistance. 
 “It’s over,” he said. “It’s only a matter of time.”
 The comments were a reflection of Israel’s deepening global isolation, with even once-staunch allies imposing or threatening economic sanctions and embargoes after years of war in Gaza and rampant violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
 With settlers advancing into areas that were previously off limits, Britain last month decried what it called “ethnic cleansing” and announced trade sanctions on settlements that it said would also apply to entities that financed their construction. Though Israel’s banking system has not been directly targeted by sanctions, a dozen countries, including Canada, France and Spain, have said they support restrictions on trade with settlements, raising the prospect of further penalties that could affect Israeli financial institutions.
 Opponents of Mr. Netanyahu’s government decried his pronouncements, which also drew a rebuke from the generally reserved central bank.
 “Crypto currencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions against Israel,” the Bank of Israel said in a statement. The bank added that the government would do better “to focus on preventing sanctions” and preserving Israel’s economic ties with its main trading partners.
 Commentators said that Mr. Netanyahu’s outlook sounded apocalyptic, and some said it was part of a scare campaign to improve his election prospects. 
 Last year, amid growing global condemnation of the Israeli military’s conduct of the war against Hamas in Gaza, where it has been accused of war crimes, and the imposition of some arms embargoes , he warned that Israel would have to become a more self-sufficient “super-Sparta.” That reference to the ancient, insular Greek city-state that practiced militaristic self-reliance was, to critics, a frightening scenario for a small country whose economy is largely driven by a tech sector that is reliant on foreign investment.
 Gadi Eisenkot, Mr. Netanyahu’s main rival in Tuesday’s election, said in a social media post that the prime minister’s “Bibi-coin vision,” a nod to cryptocurrency, would “dismantle the Israeli economy for generations.”
 “No internet purchases, no high-tech investments, no national security,” he added. 
 Yair Lapid, the opposition leader who has served as prime minister and finance minister, wrote on social media that a vote for Mr. Netanyahu was a vote for “a ruined economy, sanctions that will lead to insane price hikes, and no military alliance with the United States.” 
 And a former governor of the Bank of Israel, Jacob Frenkel, told Israel’s Channel 12 on Sunday that moving away from the international financial system would turn Israel into “a leper.” 
 Mr. Netanyahu later walked back his remarks slightly, saying that he had heard the criticism and that cryptocurrency was only one option to deal with potential financial sanctions.
 In a somewhat jarring contrast, Mr. Netanyahu’s campaign has argued that Israel’s economy overall is healthy despite years of war, helped by record export revenues, relatively low inflation and unemployment, and a strong shekel.
 But many Israelis are not feeling it. The State Comptroller, a government watchdog, warned last year that the cost of living was “skyrocketing” in part because of structural challenges in Israel’s consumer market and low competition levels.
 While foreign affairs and national security have dominated the political conversation ahead of the election, a recent survey by the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group, found that the economy was the top issue for many voters heading into Tuesday.
 Show more Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 3:18 p.m. ET Adam Rasgon 
 Reporting from Haifa, Israel Israeli elections have great consequences for Palestinians, but they don’t get to vote. 
 Image Election fliers in Beit Kahil in the West Bank on Tuesday. Credit... Erik Marmor/Getty Images The stakes of the Israeli elections are high for Palestinians in the West Bank, but they do not have the right to vote in them.
 In interviews, some Palestinians voiced objections to not being allowed to vote, especially as they felt Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was becoming more permanent.
 “The Israeli government has enormous influence over our lives,” said Montaser Amro, 32, a supermarket owner in Majd, a village near the southern city of Hebron . “It chooses when roadblocks open and close, it controls the borders, and it decides on how much of our economy functions.”
 He added, “Why can’t we vote when settlers living hundreds of meters away can?”
 Israel captured the West Bank in 1967 and reached an agreement with the Palestine Liberation Organization to establish the Palestinian Authority in the 1990s. The Palestinian Authority administers parts of the West Bank and has not held parliamentary or presidential elections for roughly 20 years .
 Many Palestinians have long hoped the Palestinian Authority would transform into an independent Palestinian state. In recent years, those hopes have dwindled. The Israeli government promotes the expansion of settlements in the West Bank that are widely considered illegal under international law and rejects Palestinian self-determination there and in Gaza. Palestinian officials have also failed to unify their ranks and renew their leadership.
 Alaa al-Khabass, 40, a resident of Hebron, said it was unjust that Palestinians could not cast ballots. 
 “Israel controls just about everything related to us, and I don’t see that changing any time soon,” he said. “We should be able to vote, but we live in painful reality where we lack rights and sovereignty.”
 Show more Oct. 27, 2026, 2:59 p.m. ET Ephrat Livni and Johnatan Reiss 
 Here are 4 things to watch for as the polls close. 
 Image Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, right, is being challenged by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar centrist political party and a former military chief of staff. Credit... Jack Guez/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images The election in Israel on Tuesday is unlikely to yield quick answers about who might lead the next government.
 Voters don’t directly pick a prime minister in Israel’s proportional parliamentary system. They choose a party or slate, the first step in determining who may be selected to try to form a government. The process is not guaranteed to succeed and can lead to another election if it does not. Here are four things to watch for.
 Turnout
 This is considered one of the most consequential elections in Israel’s history, and voters turned out in record numbers. 
 Recent polls had suggested that voter turnout could be at least as high or higher than in the last general election, in 2022. That year, slightly more than 70 percent of eligible voters — nearly 4.8 million out of nearly 6.8 million people — participated. That election followed four other votes in quick succession from 2019 to 2021 in which turnout hovered near 70 percent.
 This year, there are 7.3 million eligible voters, about 540,000 more than in 2022.
 The 3.25 percent threshold
 Parties must clear a threshold of 3.25 percent of the total vote in order to get a seat in the Knesset, or Parliament.
 But no party is expected to gain a majority of 61 parliamentary seats, according to the polls. That means there will likely be lots of post-election negotiations among those parties who pass the threshold.
 Parties or lists that do not reach the threshold lose those ballots. As a result, parties and candidates lobby voters not to waste their votes on a list that seems unlikely to meet this criterion.
 At least one party has also faced repeated attacks from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right Religious Zionism party led by Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s finance minister.
 The targeted party, People of Israel, is led by Ofer Winter, a former Israeli brigadier general with hawkish views on national security. Some polls show that much of Mr. Winter’s support comes from voters who would normally choose Likud. Mr. Winter has faced claims that a vote for his party will be wasted or may end up going to the leading challengers.
 While Mr. Winter initially said that he would support Mr. Netanyahu, he has refused any deals to withdraw from the race and has since signaled the pledge may have been premature .
 Image Ballot boxes at the headquarters of the Israeli Central Elections Committee near the central town of Shoham this month. Credit... Jack Guez/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Disinformation and challenges
 Israeli election officials have said there is no evidence of threats to the integrity of this election in terms of widespread fraud or vote counting irregularities. But experts are concerned about disinformation campaigns undermining the vote or thwarting turnout.
 Critics fear that some moves by the governing right-wing coalition may cast doubt on the outcome even before the vote happens or may thwart turnout among some voters.
 Absentee voting is mostly prohibited in Israel. But by some estimates, tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad were expected to fly in to vote, a factor that could potentially swing the outcome .
 Likud had filed a lawsuit challenging an initiative to fly in Israeli voters from abroad — a move widely perceived as an effort to limit opposition voters from showing up. The party had said the nonpartisan program provided benefits that could sway voters in violation of Israeli law. But it withdrew the suit this month after the initiative’s organizers agreed to limit flights and not to defray travelers’ costs.
 Likud and other right-wing parties also filed motions to limit participation of several Arab candidates in the election.
 The Central Elections Committee can vote to bar candidates or lists on certain grounds, such as expressing support for armed conflict against Israel. But the nation’s Supreme Court gets the final say. This month, it rejected a challenge to the Joint List, a merger of three majority-Arab parties, and to Raam, a historically Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas, who is running with Yoav Segalovitz , a former deputy minister of national security who was previously in the centrist Zionist party There Is a Future.
 Voter suppression
 In 2022, turnout in five of the largest Arab localities in Israel was lower, sometimes significantly, than the national figures. This year, officials in Arab communities worked to get voters to the polls in larger numbers and prepared for potential resistance.
 Likud and the Religious Zionism party announced plans this month to deploy thousands of religious Jewish “observers” to “prevent fraud in voting and vote-counting in Arab communities.”
 Critics contend that the presence of such observers, likely from far-right Zionist parties, was intended to intimidate Arab citizens of Israel, who make up 20 percent of the population and could be critical to the election’s outcome.
 “The main issue we want to avoid is ‘fake news,’” said Abed Shahada, who leads voter turnout efforts for an organization representing mayors and other officials in Arab localities.
 One major issue expected to drive voters is high crime in Arab communities. But if there are reports of or disinformation about criminal or violent episodes on Election Day that could keep people from the polls, Mr. Shahada said, teams are preparing by setting up a system to share verified information.

Nir Elias/Reuters Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war.
 The October 2023 assault looms large over this week’s vote. There are sharp divisions over who was to blame for failing to prevent the worst military, intelligence and policy disaster in Israel’s history.
 About 1,200 civilians and soldiers were killed that day, according to the Israeli authorities, and roughly 250 were taken hostage to Gaza. Many of the family members of hostages held by Hamas rose to prominence as they campaigned for their loved ones in television interviews and at nationwide protests.
 Most of them called for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take responsibility for the government’s failures of Oct. 7 and to prioritize negotiating the release of the hostages over continued fighting. Others supported Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government and urged it to keep up the military pressure on Hamas and Israel’s other enemies.
 Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates with a chance to win a seat in Parliament:
 Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it . As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.
 Zvi Mor , the father of a released hostage, Eitan Mor, is running as a candidate for the far-right party Religious Zionism, headed by Bezalel Smotrich. While Eitan was in captivity, Mr. Mor, an educator, founded a forum of right-wing parents of hostages and soldiers who opposed making deals with Hamas and pushed for Israel to defeat the group militarily.
 Omri Ronen , a reserve soldier, is running with the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. His grandmother, Nira Ronen, was killed in her home in Kfar Aza, one of the border communities worst hit in the October 2023 attack, along with her Filipina caregiver, Angelyn Aguirre. Before Oct. 7, Mr. Ronen had been one of the leaders of a grass-roots group of reservists protesting the government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary. He said in a recent television interview that Mr. Netanyahu, whom he called “Mr. Oct. 7,” must go. “The word responsibility has meaning,” he said.
 Rafael Ben Shitrit , a former mayor of Beit Shean in northern Israel, is in Yisrael Beitenu, a right-wing opposition party led by Avigdor Liberman. Mr. Ben Shitrit used to belong to Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party, but abandoned it after his son, Staff Sgt. Elroy Ben Shitrit, was killed in battle on Oct. 7 near the Gaza border. He has been an advocate for an independent state inquiry into what went wrong that day. Mr. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry, and the opposition parties have pledged to establish one if they are elected.
 Sharon Sharabi , also on Yisrael Beitenu’s list of candidates, is the brother of Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who was released from Gaza only to learn that his wife and two teenage daughters had been killed during the Oct. 7 attack. Another brother, Yossi Sharabi, was also taken hostage and killed after 100 days in captivity. Sharon Sharabi campaigned tirelessly for his brothers’ return. When Eli Sharabi was finally released, many Israelis were outraged over how emaciated he looked. “I was shocked,” Sharon said at the time. “I’d been told he would be thin, but I didn’t imagine how thin. It was extreme.”
 Tali Gvili , running with Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, is the mother of Master Sgt.  Support for Israel is waning among Democrats in Congress. 
 Image Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and Speaker Mike Johnson meeting in Washington last year. Credit... Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times For decades, Israel had virtually unanimous support among Republicans and Democrats in Congress, a reflection of a broader consensus in the United States in favor of strong backing for the Jewish state.
 But that consensus began to fray several years ago and has recently threatened to unravel altogether as Democrats have shifted drastically and rapidly from unequivocal support for Israel, reflecting a sea change in Americans’ views.
 Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza that followed, a growing number of Democrats have been under pressure from younger and progressive voters who are a crucial part of their base.
 Lawmakers have begun rebuking Israel in ways that were once unimaginable. They have pointed to tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians killed in Gaza and focused much of their ire on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, whose actions and policies have left his country diplomatically isolated and who has become a political lightning rod in the United States. That has put at risk the bipartisan support for military aid that Israel has always counted on from American lawmakers.
 A handful of far-right Republicans and libertarians in Congress have also questioned U.S. support for Israel, raising concern about Palestinian deaths and spending American money to defend a far-off ally. But the skepticism is far more widespread among Democrats.
 The midterm elections have been shaped in part by Democratic voters’ mounting hostility toward Israel. Party leaders now view the issue as one of the major fault lines they will have to contend with next year if they win back control of Congress in November.
 Over the past year, almost half of House Democrats voted to cut off aid to Israel . Democratic leaders who have long been staunch allies have said that the U.S.-Israeli relationship needs a fundamental reset , including a rethinking of the 10-year memorandum of understanding that commits billions of dollars of annual security aid to Israel, which will soon expire.
 And Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, who is the highest-ranking Jewish official in the nation, has condemned Mr. Netanyahu on the Senate floor and called for new leadership in Israel.
 In recent weeks, top Democrats in the House and the Senate have proposed legislation that would impose sanctions on Israel for building settlements, making clear to Israeli companies and banks that they could be penalized for ties to such activity.
 Those moves are in line with what lawmakers are hearing from voters.
 A New York Times/Siena national poll conducted in May found that 74 percent of Democratic voters opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel. A Pew Research Center poll in April found that eight in 10 Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents had an unfavorable view of Israel.
